lessons.title: Pauli X Gate (Quantum NOT)
lessons.content:
Pauli X Gate (Quantum NOT)

💡 The Intuition

The Pauli-X gate is the quantum equivalent of the classical NOT gate. Think of it as flipping a qubit from |0⟩ to |1⟩ and vice versa. In the quantum world, this is a smooth rotation in the state space.

🎛️ Pauli-X Gate

Matrix Form

X = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]

Action

X|0⟩ = |1⟩, X|1⟩ = |0⟩

The quantum NOT gate - flips qubit states and maps amplitudes.

Geometric Interpretation

On the Bloch Sphere, the Pauli-X gate represents a 180° (π radians) rotation around the X-axis. This rotation swaps the North pole (|0⟩) with the South pole (|1⟩).

Classical NOT

  • • Discrete bit flip
  • • 0 → 1, 1 → 0
  • • Deterministic

Quantum X

  • • Unitary rotation
  • • Swaps amplitudes of |0⟩ and |1⟩
  • • Reversible (X² = I)

images.alt: Pauli-X as 180° rotation on Bloch sphere
images.caption: X gate rotates qubit 180° around X-axis

codeExamples.code:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(1)
qc.x(0) # Apply X gate to qubit 0
qc.draw()
codeExamples.explanation: Using Qiskit to apply a Pauli-X gate to a single qubit circuit.

keyTakeaways: Pauli-X is the quantum equivalent of the NOT gate.
It maps |0⟩ to |1⟩ and |1⟩ to |0⟩.
Geometrically, it is a 180° rotation around the X-axis of the Bloch sphere.
It is its own inverse: applying it twice returns the qubit to its original state.

lessons.title: Pauli Y & Z Gates
lessons.content:
Pauli Y & Z Gates

💡 The Intuition

While X flips bits, the Z gate flips the phase. The Y gate is a unique combination of both a bit flip and a phase flip, involving complex numbers.

🎛️ Pauli-Y Gate

Matrix Form

Y = [[0, -i], [i, 0]]

Action

Y|0⟩ = i|1⟩, Y|1⟩ = -i|0⟩

🎛️ Pauli-Z Gate

Matrix Form

Z = [[1, 0], [0, -1]]

Action

Z|0⟩ = |0⟩, Z|1⟩ = -|1⟩

⚠️ Important

The Z gate does not change the probability of measuring 0 or 1, because |-1|² = 1. It only changes the relative phase, which is crucial for quantum interference.

images.alt: Y and Z rotations on Bloch sphere
images.caption: Y and Z gates represent 180° rotations around their respective axes.

codeExamples.code:
qc.y(0) # Apply Y gate
qc.z(0) # Apply Z gate
codeExamples.explanation: Applying Y and Z gates in Qiskit.

keyTakeaways: Y gate is a 180° rotation around the Y-axis.
Z gate is a 180° rotation around the Z-axis (Phase Flip).
Z|1⟩ results in -|1⟩, introducing a phase of π.
Pauli gates {X, Y, Z} along with Identity {I} form a basis for single-qubit operators.

lessons.title: The Hadamard Gate
lessons.content:
The Hadamard Gate

💡 The Intuition

The Hadamard gate is the "superposition creator." It takes a definite state like |0⟩ and puts it into a 50/50 blend of |0⟩ and |1⟩. It is the bridge between the computational basis and the diagonal basis.

H = 1/√2 [[1, 1], [1, -1]]

🎛️ Hadamard Action

  • H|0⟩ = |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2
  • H|1⟩ = |−⟩ = (|0⟩ - |1⟩)/√2

The Hadamard gate is its own inverse (H² = I). If you apply Hadamard to a superposition state |+⟩, you get back |0⟩. This property is used in almost every quantum algorithm to move between bases.

images.caption: Hadamard gate as a rotation around the X+Z axis.

codeExamples.explanation: Applying the Hadamard gate to qubit 0.

keyTakeaways: Hadamard creates equal superpositions from basis states.
It is a fundamental building block for quantum parallelism.
Applying H twice returns the state to the original computational basis.

lessons.title: Phase Gates: S, T, and Their Daggers
lessons.content:
Phase Gates: S, T, and Daggers

💡 The Intuition

Phase gates don't change measurement probabilities—they only modify the relative phase. Think of them as "tuning" the quantum state's rotation around the Z-axis without changing the latitude on the Bloch sphere.

S Gate (π/2)

[[1, 0], [0, i]]

90° Z-rotation

T Gate (π/4)

[[1, 0], [0, e^(iπ/4)]]

45° Z-rotation

The Dagger gates (S†, T†) perform the same rotation but in the opposite direction (clockwise vs counter-clockwise).

images.alt: S and T phase gates on Bloch sphere
images.caption: Phase gates S (90°) and T (45°) rotate around the Z-axis

codeExamples.code:
qc.s(0)  # S gate
qc.sdg(0) # S-dagger gate
qc.t(0)  # T gate

keyTakeaways: S gate is the square root of Z (S² = Z).
T gate is the square root of S (T² = S).
Phase gates only affect the relative phase of the |1⟩ component.
T gates are essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

lessons.title: Rotation Gates: Rx, Ry, Rz
lessons.content:
Rotation Gates: Rx, Ry, Rz

💡 The Intuition

Rotation gates let you move to ANY point on the Bloch sphere. They are parameterized, meaning you provide an angle θ to define how far to rotate.

Parameterized Matrices

Ry(θ) = [[cos(θ/2), -sin(θ/2)], [sin(θ/2), cos(θ/2)]]

By combining rotations around different axes (Euler angles), we can reach any arbitrary single-qubit state from |0⟩.

codeExamples.code:
import numpy as np
qc.rx(np.pi/2, 0) # Rotate 90 degrees around X
qc.ry(np.pi/4, 0) # Rotate 45 degrees around Y

keyTakeaways: Rx, Ry, Rz allow for continuous rotations.
The angle θ in the matrix is divided by 2 due to the Bloch sphere geometry.
Any single qubit gate can be decomposed into Rz and Ry rotations.
Essential for Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQA).

lessons.title: Multi-Qubit Systems & Tensor Products
lessons.content:
Multi-Qubit Systems

💡 The Intuition

When we have 2 qubits, the state space grows exponentially. While 1 qubit has 2 basis states, 2 qubits have 4: |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, and |11⟩.

To describe the state of multiple qubits, we use the Tensor Product (⊗). If qubit A is in state |ψ⟩ and qubit B is in state |φ⟩, the combined system is |ψ⟩ ⊗ |φ⟩.

|0⟩ ⊗ |1⟩ = [1, 0]ᵀ ⊗ [0, 1]ᵀ = [0, 1, 0, 0]ᵀ = |01⟩

codeExamples.code:
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.x(1)
# This creates the state |+1>
codeExamples.explanation: A 2-qubit circuit where gates act independently.

keyTakeaways: N qubits require a vector of size 2^N to describe.
The tensor product combines individual qubit states into a global state.
Standard ordering in Qiskit is qn...q1q0 (Little Endian).
Independent gates on different qubits are also combined via tensor products.

lessons.title: CNOT Gate & Entanglement
lessons.content:
CNOT Gate & Entanglement

💡 The Intuition

CNOT is the "if-then" of quantum computing. IF the control qubit is |1⟩, THEN flip the target qubit. This interaction is the key to creating Entanglement.

🎛️ CNOT (Controlled-NOT)

Maps |c, t⟩ to |c, c ⊕ t⟩

  • |00⟩ → |00⟩
  • |01⟩ → |01⟩
  • |10⟩ → |11⟩ (Flip!)
  • |11⟩ → |10⟩ (Flip!)

Creating a Bell State

By applying a Hadamard to the first qubit and then a CNOT, we create the state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. This state cannot be written as a product of two individual qubits—they are entangled.

images.caption: The control qubit (dot) and target qubit (plus sign).

codeExamples.code:
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1) # Control=0, Target=1
qc.draw()
codeExamples.explanation: Creating the maximally entangled Bell state.

keyTakeaways: CNOT is a 2-qubit gate that creates conditional logic.
Entanglement means the state of one qubit is tied to another.
CNOT is its own inverse.
It is the primary gate used to generate quantum correlations.

lessons.title: Toffoli & CCX Gates
lessons.content:
Toffoli & CCX Gates

💡 The Intuition

The Toffoli gate (CCX) is a CNOT with TWO controls. It only flips the target if BOTH control qubits are in state |1⟩. It is the quantum version of the classical AND/NAND gate.

🎛️ CCX Gate

Action: |c1, c2, t⟩ → |c1, c2, t ⊕ (c1 AND c2)⟩

The Toffoli gate is universal for classical computation, meaning any classical circuit can be built using only Toffoli gates. In quantum computing, it's used for arithmetic and oracles.

images.caption: Toffoli gate with two control qubits and one target qubit

codeExamples.explanation: Applying a Toffoli gate in Qiskit.

keyTakeaways: Toffoli is a 3-qubit gate.
It performs a controlled-controlled-NOT operation.
It is reversible, unlike the classical AND gate.
Used to implement classical logic inside quantum algorithms.

lessons.title: Circuit Composition & Design
lessons.content:
Circuit Composition & Design

Quantum algorithms are built by composing gates in sequence (time) and in parallel (space). Understanding how gates interact is vital for optimization.

Circuit Depth

The depth of a circuit is the number of time steps required to execute it. Parallel gates on different qubits do not increase depth.

⚠️ Important

Real quantum hardware has limited connectivity. Often, a CNOT can only be applied between specific physical qubits, requiring 'SWAP' gates to move information.

codeExamples.code:
qc = QuantumCircuit(2)
qc.h(0)
qc.x(1)
qc.cx(0, 1)
print(f"Circuit Depth: {qc.depth()}")
codeExamples.explanation: Measuring the depth of a simple circuit.

keyTakeaways: Gates are applied from left to right in a circuit diagram.
Circuit depth affects the impact of decoherence and noise.
Complex gates are often decomposed into a native gate set (e.g., Rz, Sx, CNOT).
Optimization involves reducing the number of CNOT gates.

lessons.title: Gates Quiz
lessons.content:
Quantum Gates Mastery Quiz

Test your knowledge of single and multi-qubit gates.

1. Which gate creates an equal superposition from |0⟩?

  • A) Pauli-X
  • B) Pauli-Z
  • C) Hadamard
  • D) S Gate

2. What is the result of applying H then Z then H to the state |0⟩?

  • A) |0⟩
  • B) |1⟩
  • C) |+⟩
  • D) |−⟩
keyTakeaways: Review the matrix forms of X, Y, Z, and H.
Understand the geometric effect of rotations.
Recall the action of CNOT on basis states.
Identify the relationship between S, T, and Z gates.
